# Studyflow: a BPMN-based visual notation for end-to-end specification of experimental research in cognitive sciences

**Authors:**
Morteza Ansarinia^1,\*^ (ORCID 0000-0001-8335-6704),
Hoorieh Afkari Roshan^1^ (ORCID 0000-0003-4787-8331),
Pedro Cardoso-Leite^1^ (ORCID 0000-0002-2848-5527)

^1^ University of Luxembourg, Luxembourg
^\*^ Corresponding author: morteza.ansarinia@uni.lu

## Abstract

A scientific study passes through many hands: researcher, ethics committee, participant, data engineer, analyst, reviewer, replicator; and each typically receives a different artifact: a protocol PDF, an experiment script, a preprocessing notebook, a manuscript figure, a CONSORT diagram. These artifacts drift apart, and no single representation describes the study as it was actually run. We present **Studyflow**, a notation that closes this gap by extending Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) with elements specific to experimental cognitive sciences: domain-specific activities (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction), decision gateways (randomization, eligibility criteria), data operations (map, filter, reduce), and data elements bound to community practices (BIDS, Psych-DS, BDM, CSVW). A single `.studyflow` file serves as protocol, specification, publication figure, and participant-facing application. We describe the language, an open-source modeler, and a runner, and follow one reproducible study through its full lifecycle, from protocol design to publication: a battery of cognitive tasks administered to human participants and a panel of artificial agents, then compared across tasks, models, and personas.

## Impact statement

Studyflow turns a scientific study into a single source-of-truth diagram that can be reviewed, executed, and published, replacing the divergent artifacts (protocols, scripts, pipeline parameters, reporting diagrams) that currently fragment experimental research across stakeholders.

## Keywords

scientific workflows; experimental design; BPMN; reproducibility; process modeling

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 The reproducibility gap is in *processes*, not just data

A scientific study touches many people and systems. A researcher designs it; an ethics committee approves it; a participant runs it; a data pipeline ingests it; a model trains on it; a reviewer reads it in a manuscript; a replicator tries to rebuild it. Reproducing the study after the fact requires more than the data and the manuscript: it requires an explicit, complete description of the *processes* that generated them [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines]. A complete description of any computing system needs both a data model and a process model [@Sehgal2011]; in cognitive sciences, however, most standardization effort has gone into data, leaving the processes that produce the data documented in narrative prose, ad-hoc lab conventions, box-and-arrow diagrams, or code repositories that drift apart from the prose they accompany [@bell2021perspectives; @osc2015].

The cost of this missing process model is visible whenever a study has to be re-read by anyone other than its author. The researcher's protocol PDF, the ethics application, the experiment script, the preprocessing notebook, the model card, the manuscript figure, and the CONSORT diagram begin as different views of the same study and end as inconsistent ones. By the end, no single artifact describes the study *as it was actually run*. Trust in research, and increasingly trust in code and data on which research depends, is built or lost precisely at this point of divergence.

The mechanism most often used to compensate for missing process models is voluntary, narrative reporting (checklists, pre-registration forms, journal endorsements), and the empirical record on whether it works is now available. A cross-sectional study of 400 psychology articles published in 2022 found that only 7%-14% had been preregistered and only 14%-16% shared raw data, despite more than a decade of reform initiatives [@hardwicke2024prevalence]. The pattern is not limited to psychology: ARRIVE 2.0 explicitly documents that endorsement by more than 1000 journals failed to improve adherence [@percie2020arrive], and a randomized controlled trial at *PLOS ONE* found that requesting a completed checklist at submission did not improve reporting compliance either [@hair2019iicarus]. Even at journals that have moved transparency from opt-in to default policy, the shift required explicit editorial mandates rather than voluntary uptake [@hardwicke2024transparency]. The conclusion is not that researchers are uncooperative but that narrative checklists are the wrong instrument: they specify *what to mention* without requiring *what to actually share*, as they accept a narrative description of processes instead of formal, verifiable ones. Consequently, they leave the underlying process model implicit and open to interpretation.

We argue that reproducibility should be a property of the shared artifact itself rather than a separate documentation maintained alongside the work. A single, machine-readable, human-understandable representation of a study, shared across its many audiences, would force the process model and the data model to stay aligned. The contribution of this paper is one concrete realization of that idea, grounded in a standard process notation and a working open source tool that can be replaced by others without losing the underlying specification.

## 1.2 Current practice fragments the study across artifacts

Today, the audiences of science each receive a different artifact, and each artifact drifts from the rest. We can organize current approaches into four overlapping families.

**Box-and-arrow figures** in manuscripts communicate study logic at a glance but are not standardized, not machine-verifiable, and rarely connect to the code that runs the study. They are tailored to each stakeholder (a CONSORT flow for a journal, a slide deck for a funding agency, a sketch on a whiteboard for an engineer) and so are difficult to keep mutually consistent [@bogale2024]. **Checklists and pre-registration forms** (cataloged through the EQUATOR network [@simera2010equator]) address the need for structured text but encode it in free-form fields, in binary format or proprietary PDF or DOCX, on data silos that resist version control. **Data standards, ontologies, and packages** (BIDS, Psych-DS, the Behaverse Data Model, CSVW [@bids; @psychds; @bdm; @csvw]) make the data side machine-readable but say little about the processes that produced the data, and ontology-based process models [@norouzi2025semantic_processes], while numerous, demand high upfront effort and are rarely reused. **Code and configuration** (analysis scripts, GitHub Actions, Nextflow [@kinsman2021], registries such as protocols.io [@teytelman2016]) make pipelines precise but require domain-specific programming literacy that excludes ethics boards, reviewers, and many collaborators.

The recurring pattern is a split between **execution** and **communication**: tools that execute the study (scripts, workflow engines, CI pipelines) target developers and machines; tools that communicate the study (protocol PDFs, narrative platforms, reporting checklists) target humans. Provenance systems track the computational graph well but rarely capture the full experimental context (randomization decisions, manual annotations, protocol deviations) which creates a boundary between a well-tracked computational graph and a partially represented experimental graph [@souza2020provenance; @simmons2018provenance_sport]. No single representation currently spans the full lifecycle of a study in a form that scientists, engineers, funding agencies, ethics boards, and journal editors can all read, validate, and execute (Figure 1).

## 1.3 BPMN as a foundation

The domain (designing, executing, and reporting experiments in cognitive sciences) meets the standard criteria for building a domain-specific modeling language (DSL): recurring structural patterns across studies, expert users who would benefit from a familiar notation rather than general-purpose code, and the absence of an executable language that already covers the experiment lifecycle end-to-end [@mernik2005dsl]. Rather than invent a new graphical language for cognitive experiments, we extend an established one whose visual conventions have already been adopted in other domains. The principles that distinguish an effective visual notation from a merely correct one are themselves a research subject [@moody2009physics], and a notation that researchers, engineers, and reviewers already recognize is a cheaper starting point.

Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is a mature ISO-standard graphical language for processes [@white2004introduction]. It already provides what scientific workflows need at the structural level: events, activities, sub-processes, decision making (gateways), data objects, sequence and data flows, and choreography between participants. It has an established tooling ecosystem (editors such as `bpmn-js` and Camunda Modeler, drawing libraries such as diagrams.net) and a body of accumulated practice in industries where process clarity is not optional. Building on BPMN gives any domain-specific extension a vocabulary that engineers and analysts already recognize, plus a standard serialization (BPMN 2.0 XML) that survives any single tool.

BPMN's extension mechanisms (`extensionElements` and namespaced attributes) is the bridge we use. The standard permits domain-specific elements and attributes to be added inside a new namespace; a BPMN-only parser ignores them gracefully, while a domain-aware tool can validate and render them [@magnani2009bpdmn]. Existing BPMN extensions in other domains demonstrate the pattern: BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless machine-learning pipelines [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], extensions for human-AI collaboration [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent], and applications to healthcare more broadly [@pufahl2022]. A systematic review identifies dozens more profiles across domains [@zarour2019], and a complementary taxonomy classifies how such extensions relate to the BPMN core [@braun2014classification]. Cognitive and behavioral research is visibly absent from this list.

<!-- 
Recent large-language-model-assisted BPMN authoring tools (ProMoAI, BPMN-ChatBot, and related work [@kourani2024promoai; @kourani2024process_modeling_llm]) accelerate diagram authoring from text, but evaluations show that competitive syntactic quality does not translate into domain-specific semantics or domain-specific validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Authoring help is welcome; it is not a substitute for a profile that defines what *cognitive task*, *random assignment*, or *eligibility check* mean inside a process model. That profile is the gap Studyflow fills. -->

## 1.4 Contributions

We contribute five artifacts, each independently usable:

1. **A versioned language specification** for Studyflow, authored as a LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that serves as the single source of truth for element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules. LinkML is a schema-modeling framework increasingly adopted across biology, biomedicine, and ontology engineering, and provides FAIR-aligned [@fair] serialization plus tooling for documentation, validator, and downstream-converter generation. The Studyflow LinkML schema is independent of any particular implementation: a third party can target it directly without depending on the modeler's code.

2. **A layered set of runtime schemas** mirroring the LinkML specification in the YAML format that BPMN tooling consumes, comprising the language core, a companion cognitive layer, and four optional domain extensions (the Behaverse cognitive battery, a generic process orchestration layer, a large-scale data transformation layer, and a multimodal acquisition layer for EEG and eye tracking). New domain semantics plug in without touching the core.

3. **A library of worked example diagrams** that ship with the modeler, including a complete CONSORT 2025 randomized-trial template, a SPIRIT 2025 protocol schedule, and patterns for cognitive tasks, data collection, analysis pipelines, MLOps, multi-agent choreography, and reporting guidelines.

4. **The Studyflow Modeler**, an open-source client-side web application (MIT-licensed) for authoring, inspecting, simulating, validating, and publishing Studyflow diagrams. Its inspector and palette are generated from the schemas, so the language and the editor stay in sync.

5. **The Studyflow Runner**, a separate client-side application that parses, validates, and walks a Studyflow file step by step. It ships with built-in renderers for consents, instructions, questionnaire instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II), generic tasks, and embedded Behaverse cognitive-task runtimes; supports seeded determinism for reproducible random branches; and drives human participants, classic agents (via CogEnv), and language-model agents from the same diagram.

# 2. Results

Studyflow's working artifacts are a language, a modeler, and a runner, and a single `.studyflow` source feeds all three while rendering three ways (Study, Gantt, Checklist) for different readers. We exercise them on one study that administers a battery of cognitive tasks to both human participants and a panel of artificial agents. Every stage of that study, from protocol to publication, reads and writes the same source, so the protocol an ethics board approves is the one participants run, the one the analysis consumes, and the one the published figure is exported from.

## 2.1 The Studyflow language

Studyflow is a domain-specific profile of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0 [@white2004introduction] tailored to experimental research in cognitive sciences. We adopted BPMN as the host notation rather than inventing a new language for three reasons. First, Studyflow diagrams remain valid BPMN 2.0 XML and open in any compliant tool (Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io, diagrams.net), with Studyflow-specific elements degrading gracefully. Second, BPMN's flowchart-like visual grammar is already familiar to many researchers, lowering adoption barriers; readers new to flowcharts still face a learning curve, but a shallower one than a custom language would impose. Third, BPMN provides a formal extension mechanism (`extensionElements`, namespaced attributes) for adding domain semantics without breaking the base standard [@stroppi2011; @magnani2009bpdmn].

**What Studyflow inherits.** Studyflow reuses BPMN's full vocabulary for control flow and structure: start, end, intermediate, boundary, timer, and error *events*; tasks, sub-processes, and call activities; exclusive, parallel, inclusive, event-based, and complex *gateways*; sequence flows and message flows; data objects and data stores with their associations; pools and lanes; and choreography for multi-agent interactions. These elements render with standard BPMN shapes and behave as specified by the OMG.

**What Studyflow adds.** Four areas extend BPMN with vocabulary that experimental research routinely needs. First, a top-level **study container** groups every other element and carries study-level metadata (title, version, authors, runtime). Second, **domain-specific activity types** specialize the generic BPMN task with research-meaningful kinds (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest periods, video games, and the curated Behaverse cognitive battery), each rendering with a distinctive icon while remaining a normal BPMN task underneath. Third, **research-specific data elements** augment BPMN's generic data objects with bindings to community schemas (BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], the Behaverse Data Model, CSVW), and a small **data-operations vocabulary** (map, filter, reduce, group, transform, compose) renders the *kind* of transformation as a task marker, so how data flows is visible at a glance. Fourth, **research gateways** encode the branching patterns specific to experimental design: a random gateway for randomization, a stratified-allocation gateway, and an eligibility gateway that lists inclusion and exclusion criteria. Optional temporal attributes (onset, duration, progress) attached to activities and events let the Gantt view derive trial schedules and visit calendars from the same diagram.

**What Studyflow deliberately leaves alone.** Studyflow does not redefine BPMN's serialization conventions: XML namespaces, element identifiers, and the base shape vocabulary are untouched. Domain extensions live inside BPMN's native extension slot, so a generic BPMN renderer ignores them gracefully while a Studyflow-aware tool validates and renders them consistently.

**A layered set of schemas.** The vocabulary is partitioned into a small core and optional domain extensions that can be loaded on demand (Figure 2). The core covers the language scaffolding (study container, events, sequence flows, base activity, data infrastructure) plus a companion cognitive layer (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest, video games, research gateways). Four optional layers cover specific domains (the Behaverse Unity battery, generic process orchestration, large-scale data transformation, and multimodal acquisition for EEG and eye tracking), and new domains plug in by authoring a schema without modifying the core. The complete element catalog is in Supplementary Table S1.

## 2.2 The Studyflow Modeler

The **Studyflow Modeler** is an open-source web application (MIT-licensed) that implements the Studyflow language for authoring, inspecting, simulating, and publishing diagrams. It runs entirely in the browser with no server dependency. Two design choices shape the modeler. First, the language specification is maintained as a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] independent of the modeler codebase, so third-party tools (linters, converters, execution engines) can target the same specification. The modeler tracks the schema rather than owning it. Second, the user interface is **schema-driven**: palette entries, the inspector panel, and validation rules are generated from the layered moddle schemas. Adding an element type or attribute to a schema updates the UI automatically, which keeps the modeler lightweight as the notation evolves with community feedback.

The authoring workflow (Figure 3) proceeds in seven steps. (1) **Sign in.** Users open the hosted modeler. A Behaverse API key unlocks publish; guest mode supports draft-only authoring. (2) **Drag from the palette.** The left palette exposes the BPMN base vocabulary alongside the Studyflow-specific elements (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction, random gateway, eligibility gateway, dataset, etc.); optional schemas can be toggled from the palette settings. (3) **Edit in the inspector.** Selecting an element opens a right-hand inspector sidebar whose fields are derived from the element's schema entry: required attributes are flagged, enumerated values become dropdowns, markdown fields render with a preview, and conditional attributes appear only when their predicate holds. (4) **Connect elements.** The connect tool wires sequence flows, data associations, and message flows; the modeler picks the appropriate edge type from the source/target pair. (5) **Save and export.** Diagrams persist as `.studyflow` files (BPMN 2.0 XML with Studyflow extensions in named namespaces) so they diff cleanly in Git and remain valid BPMN. Export to PNG and SVG produces publication-ready figures; SVGs can embed the source XML for one-file commits. (6) **Simulate.** A simulation mode steps through the diagram interactively, exercising gateway logic and showing the next admissible elements, useful for catching dead branches and missing conditions before a study runs. (7) **Publish.** *File → Publish* uploads the diagram to the Behaverse Data Server [@bds], which renders its own participant-facing UI from the diagram structure (local layout in the modeler is for human readers; the server ignores it). Local stimuli must be referenced by URL or uploaded separately. Each publish creates a new server-side version, so studies already in the field do not break when authors push updates, and earlier versions remain reachable by identifier.

This separation between specification (the LinkML schema), authoring tool (the modeler), runtime UI (the data server), and visual layout (export artifacts) lets each component evolve independently while a single `.studyflow` source ties them together.

## 2.3 The Studyflow Runner

The **Studyflow Runner** is a distinct client-side application that takes a Studyflow diagram and walks a participant (or an artificial agent) through it node by node. It lives alongside the modeler. A diagram reaches it three ways: from the modeler's *Run* button, by URL parameter when the diagram is hosted somewhere, or by direct file upload. An optional random seed makes any branching deterministic, so pilot runs and regression tests are reproducible.

After loading, the runner parses the diagram, validates it node by node, and traverses it from start to end. Validation is layered: type-level constraints (required attributes, enumerated values, conditional visibility) are checked at parse time; structural constraints (every start has an outgoing flow, every gateway is fully wired, every flow has a valid source and target) are checked by the modeler at edit time; per-step validators (a questionnaire needs an instrument, a Behaverse cognitive task needs a paradigm identifier) run before traversal begins. The same per-step validators are exposed to the modeler's lint pass, so authors see the errors they would see at run time. Each visited node yields a step that the runner renders and waits to complete; when the end event is reached, the run finishes and any completion code or redirect specified in the diagram takes effect.

**Gateway semantics.** Random gateways select an outgoing branch uniformly at random under the seed. Stratified allocation currently falls back to the same uniform pick; balanced stratification is roadmap work. Exclusive and inclusive gateways evaluate conditions against a runtime variable store that nodes can write to as they execute, with fallback to a default branch when no condition matches. Parallel gateways are not yet supported.

**Built-in step kinds.** Six kinds ship: a **start** node that shows a consent screen when one is attached, an **end** node that issues a completion code and an optional redirect, an **instruction** node that renders markdown, a **questionnaire** node with built-in instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II) plus custom instruments via inline schema, a **Behaverse cognitive-task** node that embeds the Behaverse Unity runtime and supports three response sources (Unity's in-game bot, runner-side uniform random, or a language-model call per trial), and a **generic-task** fallback. Element kinds that are not steps in the participant flow (data references, model-only sub-processes) are skipped at run time, since they affect modeling and analysis, not execution.

**Runtime extensibility.** New step kinds plug in by adding one folder to the runner's node directory: a small matcher selects which diagram elements the kind handles, a mapper extracts the runtime parameters from the element, and a React component renders the step. A domain group can thus ship a custom step (an eye-tracking calibration, a VR scene) without forking the runner. The runner's curated step set, absent parallel-gateway support, and the stratified-allocation fallback to uniform random are scope choices rather than language limitations: the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time, and each gap maps to a roadmap item.

Figure 4 [GAP: a four-to-six-panel walkthrough of a participant moving from consent through an instruction, a questionnaire, and a Behaverse cognitive task to the end screen, on the same diagram authored in §2.2.]

## 2.4 The three views: Study / Gantt / Checklist

A single `.studyflow` source is rendered three ways, each tuned to a different stakeholder need (Figure 5). The three views read the same file, so changes propagate automatically.

**Study view.** The default rendering: a BPMN-like graph showing every element and connection. The Study view is *structural*; it shows what happens and in what order but does not commit to wall-clock timing. It is the canonical view for Methods sections, for reviewers checking logical structure, and for pipeline authors wiring up data flow.

**Gantt view.** A Gantt-style rendering that places time-sensitive elements along a temporal axis. BPMN has timer events but no native way to express activity duration, scheduled onset, or progress. Studyflow attaches these as optional attributes on BPMN activities and events: **onset**, **duration**, and **progress** (percentage or label). Resource allocation is expressed directly as BPMN pools and lanes, which the Gantt uses to group rows; there is no separate `resourceAllocation` attribute. When the temporal attributes are present, the Gantt view renders the diagram automatically. The same mechanism scales from trial-level timing (stimulus duration, ITI, response window) to study-level timing (visit schedule, follow-ups). Milestones are the special case of zero duration, and hierarchical Gantt structures map directly onto BPMN sub-processes. The Gantt view is useful for longitudinal studies and SPIRIT-style schedules of enrolment and assessment [@spirit2013].

**Checklist view.** A task-oriented view that flattens the diagram into a list of activities with their associated items and status. Every Studyflow element carries an optional `checklist` attribute (a markdown list) that the Checklist view extracts and aggregates. The view supports two uses: *running studies day-to-day* (what is next, what is done) and *adhering to reporting guidelines* (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA, CARE), where guideline items are mapped to the diagram elements that satisfy them so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. Checklists ship with the `.studyflow` file and can be exported to JSON or Markdown for external task managers.

| If you need to communicate... | Use |
|---|---|
| Procedural structure, branching, data flow | Study view |
| Wall-clock timing, schedules, durations | Gantt view |
| Coverage against a reporting checklist or protocol | Checklist view |

A single `.studyflow` source thus supports three reading paths (a methods diagram, a project schedule, a reporting audit) without forcing authors to maintain three artifacts that drift apart.


## 2.5 Design: the protocol, randomization, and reporting scaffolding

Our worked example is a single study that administers a battery of cognitive tasks to human participants and a panel of artificial agents, then compares them across tasks. We design it as a randomized controlled trial so the protocol carries the scaffolding a registered study needs: consent, eligibility screening, random allocation (here, counterbalanced task order across the battery), and the structure a journal will later expect. In current practice that scaffolding is spread across a registry entry, an ethics PDF, a recruitment system, and a CONSORT flow diagram drawn at write-up time, none of which is a machine-readable view of the others [@moher2012; @rennie2001; @hopewell2025consort]. The flow diagram in particular is a participant-tracking schematic, with enrollment, allocation, follow-up, and analysis as its four canonical rows and attrition counts annotating each transition; it is a *document* about the trial, not the *spec* that drove it. Studyflow makes the document and the spec one file.

We start from the CONSORT 2025 reference diagram that ships with the modeler, which authors can fork, parameterize, and run as the actual protocol of a new trial [@hopewell2025consort]. Figure 6 contrasts three artifacts: (a) the canonical CONSORT 2025 reference flow as published by the CONSORT group, (b) a Studyflow reproduction encoded with the same labels and pathways, and (c) an annotated comparison whose left path uses Studyflow boundary error events and whose right path uses the traditional text-and-box treatment.

The crucial mechanical difference is how attrition is represented. In the traditional figure, each "Excluded / Did not receive / Lost to follow-up / Discontinued" box is an unconnected annotation sitting next to the column of follow-up activities, and readers infer that these counts subtract from the main flow. In the Studyflow diagram, attrition is encoded as a *boundary error event* attached to the activity from which participants departed: exclusion at screening hangs off the eligibility gateway, non-receipt of intervention off the two allocation tasks, loss to follow-up and discontinuation off the follow-up tasks, and exclusion from analysis off the analysis tasks. Each event terminates in an error end event with a labeled count. This has three consequences. The topology of the diagram now matches the topology of the trial: a participant lost during follow-up exits along an edge whose origin is the follow-up activity itself, not an arrow drawn from a side annotation. Summing attrition becomes a graph operation rather than a manual exercise, so a Studyflow-aware validator can verify that no row's outbound counts exceed its inbound count. And the boundary error event is the same primitive BPMN uses to model interrupts in any business process, so the diagram remains valid BPMN 2.0 and inherits the standard execution semantics for error handling [@stroppi2011; @ait2024bpmn_humanagent].

The diagram carries domain semantics alongside the BPMN scaffolding. The enrollment start event references a participant-facing consent PDF, so a runner that reaches this node renders the consent screen automatically before any randomization happens. The screening task carries a markdown checklist (demographic intake, medical history, baseline cognitive screen) that also drives the Checklist view. The eligibility gateway and the randomization gateway are typed as such, and the battery's tasks each declare themselves as cognitive tasks with their own inline parameter block (for the n-back, the N level, stimulus duration, inter-trial interval, and trials per block). Allocation, follow-up, and analysis tasks each carry their own checklists describing protocol obligations. A single file therefore serves four readers at once: the trial registry (a registered protocol with explicit randomization and eligibility criteria), the ethics board (consent content and per-task checklists), the data-collection platform (the embedded cognitive-task instrument and its parameters), and the journal (the CONSORT figure with attrition flows already wired). The mechanism is BPMN's standard extension protocol [@stroppi2011], with each reader interpreting the layer it cares about; what is new is that the union of those layers, rendered together, *is* a CONSORT diagram.

Where CONSORT structures the *report*, SPIRIT structures the *plan*. The same study renders as a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, from a worked SPIRIT template the modeler ships, whose 34 checklist items across 9 topics project onto the Gantt view [@chan2025spirit; @spirit2013]. A SPIRIT plan and a CONSORT report are then the same file at two points in its lifecycle: the schedule before randomization, and the flow diagram with attrition counts written into the labels of the boundary error events once the study has run.

## 2.6 Collect: one diagram, many executors

Data collection is where Studyflow's central move becomes concrete: *who executes the protocol is a runtime decision, not a property of the diagram*. Our study administers a six-task battery drawn from the Behaverse suite, spanning working memory (n-back and digit span), attention (multiple-object tracking), processing speed (pattern comparison), fluid reasoning (matrix reasoning), and set-shifting (card sorting). One `.studyflow` source drives every task and every executor. The n-back is a near-universal probe of working memory [@bell2021perspectives] and serves as the worked example below; the other five ride the same machinery.

**The round-trip.** We authored the battery in the Studyflow Modeler, saving it as one Studyflow diagram that orchestrates consent, baseline questionnaires, and a sequence of the six tasks, each a Behaverse cognitive-task node, with order counterbalanced across participants, then loaded that file into the Studyflow Runner. Each task is itself a Behaverse timeline of blocks (a warm-up, the test blocks, and any adaptive staircase), so the battery is a nested structure that prose and slides flatten but the diagram keeps explicit. The runner validates that every task's required parameters are present before traversal begins, then walks the diagram one node at a time (Figure 4). Instructions render as markdown, the questionnaire that precedes the task uses a built-in instrument (PHQ-9, GAD-7, and BDI-II all ship; custom instruments are accepted via inline schema), and trial-level execution is delegated to the Behaverse Unity runtime through the Behaverse cognitive-task node. Seeded randomization, set as a URL parameter (`?seed=42`), makes the within-task sequence and every random branch deterministic, which is the property that lets a pilot dataset be reproduced exactly from the same source.

**Encoding the trials.** Figure 7 places the traditional slide-style N-back figure next to the Studyflow equivalent. The slide is intuitive but underdetermined: timing values often live only in the caption, the boundary between trial and block is implicit, and decisions like "what counts as a correct match" are buried in the analysis code. Studyflow authors the trial as an explicit subgraph instead, with a stimulus activity, a boundary timer for the response window, a second boundary timer for the inter-trial interval, and text annotations labeling the target and non-target branches. The trial-by-trial encoding in Figure 7 is pedagogical; for execution beyond a handful of trials the same logic compresses into a single Behaverse cognitive task whose inline configuration declares the N level, stream specification, trial count, stimulus duration, and inter-trial interval, and which the runner expands into individual trials via the Behaverse Unity runtime. The XML excerpt in Figure 7c shows how these primitives serialize. The same compression applies to every task in the battery: each is one Behaverse cognitive-task node whose inline timeline, blocks, stop rules, and optional staircase the runtime expands into trials. Each trial the runner emits is logged to the Behaverse Data Model trials-level schema [@bdm], which is Psych-DS-compatible [@psychds], so the same diagram produces a CSV whose columns are predetermined by the schema and whose semantic content is determined by the diagram, identically across all six tasks. The trials CSV is reviewable side by side with the diagram, and a third party with only those two files can reconstruct what each row means without running the modeler.

**Three kinds of executor.** The same source reaches three runtimes today, each through a different adapter and all emitting trials under the common schema (Figure 12). *Human participants* run through the Behaverse Data Server: the author publishes the diagram, the server renders its own participant-facing UI from the diagram structure, and the trials log out under the schema. *Classic reinforcement-learning agents* run through CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv], which administers Behaverse cognitive tasks to RL policies via DeepMind's AndroidEnv layer, exposing them to the same screenshots, response buttons, and time constraints a human would see [@defossez2020bdm]; running a random or scripted policy through every node also doubles as protocol validation, surfacing stuck states and timing edge cases before any human sits down. *Language-model agents* run through the runner's per-trial bridge: each trial is sent to the configured model with a free-form prompt that steers a simulated participant (persona, target accuracy, mistake rate), and vision-capable models read the on-screen frame through an optional screenshot pathway, so the battery's spatial tasks (object tracking, matrix reasoning, card sorting), which carry no useful textual stimulus, remain tractable. If a model returns an answer outside the allowed set, the runner records the mismatch and falls back to a uniform random choice, so a transient failure cannot silently corrupt the dataset.

**Profiling a panel of agents.** Because the executor is a parameter, we profile a matrix of agents against the whole battery rather than scoring one agent on one task. We cross *model* (a uniform-random baseline, a commercial vision-language model, and an open-weight model served locally for offline and HPC-side use) with *persona* (a careful "expert" aiming for near-ceiling accuracy, a "tired" participant aiming for roughly 80%, and a "fast-guesser" trading accuracy for speed) and with *task* (the six battery tasks). A single free-form prompt sets each persona, and because the prompt is independent of the stimulus, the same persona carries across the whole battery, so each model contributes a profile across constructs rather than a single score. We piloted every model-by-persona-by-task cell for [N] trials at seed 42 with no edits to the source diagram between runs (Figure 13, Table 3), which reports accuracy, median response time, and the rate at which a reply fell outside the allowed set and triggered the runner's random-fallback. The random baseline sits near chance on every task; the persona prompts move the commercial model toward their accuracy targets both on the tasks that admit a textual reading and, through the screenshot pathway, on the spatial tasks that have no textual stimulus at all; the open-weight model follows the same profile at some cost in accuracy while running without an external API. The comparison is a profile, not a scalar: it shows how faithfully each model holds a persona across constructs, how its accuracy and response-time ordering over tasks lines up against the human ordering, and where open- and closed-weight models diverge, all from one diagram and all accumulating into one table whose columns are fixed by the schema rather than by which executor produced the row. This is the "few models, many items" regime [@ansarinia2022cogtext] made tractable and extended across tasks: rather than rank many models on a single task, we vary the diagram (task, difficulty, response window, persona) and profile a handful of agents over a whole battery of parametrically related items.

**Beyond one participant.** The battery is administered to one participant at a time, but the same notation scales to designs where the *interaction itself* is the unit of analysis. Joint action has been a first-class concern in cognitive science for two decades [@sebanz2006joint], supported by dyadic decision experiments, parent-child protocols, two-player games, and hyperscanning paradigms that measure neural coupling between simultaneously recorded participants [@babiloni2014hyperscanning; @hakim2023interbrain]. BPMN 2.0's **choreography task** models exactly this, a directed exchange between participants with an explicit initiator [@pufahl2022; @decker2011choreography], which Studyflow inherits unchanged for dyadic, experimenter-driven, and parent-child patterns. Synchronization across instruments rather than people is handled one layer down by the Lab Streaming Layer, the de facto architecture for timestamped multimodal stream collection across heterogeneous devices [@kothe2025lsl]: a Studyflow diagram declares which actors interact and in what order while LSL aligns the EEG, eye-tracker, and behavioral streams it references through schema-bound datasets. The artificial-agent panel above is the same construct from a different angle. Confederate paradigms, in which a hidden agent stands in for a participant, have structured cognitive science for decades [@dahlback1993woz], and that role is now routinely filled by language models used to simulate participants and replicate published effects at scale [@aher2023llms], evaluated as cognitive subjects in their own right [@binz2023gpt3], or instantiated as generative confederates in richer environments [@park2023agents]. A choreography task between a human and an LLM agent is the same primitive as one between two humans. As LLM-driven discovery moves toward multi-agent laboratories that propose, execute, and interpret experiments end-to-end [@ghareeb2025], the case for an explicit, machine-readable procedural specification only grows. The runner does not yet traverse choreography tasks (a roadmap item), but the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time and validates against the BPMN 2.0 choreography schema [@stroppi2011].

**Honest limits.** The multi-executor composition holds today for the curated Behaverse battery (the six tasks used here plus sustained attention, useful-field-of-view, spatial cueing, simple reaction time, and others; 22 in total), because those tasks ship as Unity scenes that the Behaverse Data Server, CogEnv, and the runner all recognize. A custom PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy] or jsPsych task referenced from a Studyflow diagram is still executable for human participants, but the RL and LLM adapters would need a corresponding bridge to read its stimulus stream and inject responses. Studyflow is also not a stimulus-presentation library: rendering letters at a fixed retinal angle still requires the Behaverse Unity runtime or an external framework reached by URL. The diagram describes which stimulus to show, in what order, under what timing constraint, and what to record, not the pixel-level mechanics of showing it. Generalizing the trial-level interface beyond Behaverse Unity is a roadmap item.

## 2.7 Analyze and compare: a reproducible pipeline over human and agent trials

Analysis is where the dominant artifact is a script: an R or Python notebook with implicit dependencies, comments instead of types, and no machine-readable record of its steps. Studyflow's data operations give every script-style operation an explicit type (element-wise map, row filter, partition group, group-wise reduce, expansion, generic transform, and bundled pipeline), so the *kind* of work each step does is visible in the diagram rather than buried in code. Combined with dataset, data-store, and schema elements, the diagram is a complete, machine-readable pre-registration of the analysis.

We analyze the trials collected above. The pipeline is nine steps: read the raw trials from the dataset the runner emitted; filter invalid trials (RT < 100 ms, missing data, fallback-flagged rows); map to derived measures (log-RT, accuracy, per-task correctness codes); branch at an exclusive gateway on the comparison of interest (here, task, executor, and persona); group by task, executor, and persona; reduce to per-group accuracy, median RT, and standard errors; route through a manual review where the analyst inspects outliers and optionally re-runs with adjusted criteria; transform into a publication-ready summary; and write to a table whose schema declares every column the downstream figure depends on. Three properties are not optional: the conditional branch is visible in the topology rather than buried inside an `if`; the manual review has an explicit place in the diagram, making it harder to skip; and the schema on the output table is part of the spec rather than implicit in the column names.

The same diagram carries process and data together, which is what makes the human-versus-agent comparison auditable. Most workflow tools separate *process* (what runs, in what order) from *data* (the tables, columns, and units it consumes and produces): UML splits them into activity and class diagrams [@cuevasvicenttin2013workflows], DAG engines describe the process in code and leave data layout to convention, and reporting guidelines describe the process in prose and the data in a separate file. Studyflow puts both on one canvas. Activities sit on the sequence-flow graph while datasets, stores, catalogs, schemas, and snapshots sit on a parallel data-flow graph, connected by BPMN data associations rendered as dashed edges. Every dataset declares its format (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS, or generic) and a schema, inline or external; tabular data carries a CSVW body or a schema reference [@hoytO3GuidelinesOpen2024; @csvw], and non-tabular data documents tensor dimensions, dtypes, and units. Bindings to BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], and the Behaverse Data Model [@bdm] are typed contracts the modeler validates and the runner respects, not comments, so an analyst can verify from the diagram alone that a downstream task consumes exactly the column an upstream task produced.

Figure 8 shows the RT-analysis subprocess beside the equivalent dplyr code. The diagram encodes the same chained pipeline a tidyverse user would write as `filter |> mutate |> group_by |> summarize`, with two added commitments. First, typed inputs and outputs: the raw and summary datasets are typed (BDM trials level on the way in, models level on the way out), registered in a catalog, and physically stored in a backing store (a DuckDB-plus-Parquet ducklake in our example). Second, the analysis task's composed-operation marker declares which primitive operations the task may perform, so tooling can reject any implementation that touches an undeclared column or runs an unauthorized operation. The comparison this produces is the one collection set up: accuracy and response-time distributions across task, executor, and persona, side by side and reproducible from the seed, with the human arm slotting into the same table and schema the agents wrote to whenever human pilot data is collected.

Pre-registration of analysis is then the diagram itself. A pre-registered plan in current practice is free text on a registry website with no machine-checkable correspondence to the code eventually run. Under the Studyflow encoding the diagram is the spec, the dplyr pipeline is one valid implementation, and any divergence between the two is detectable by inspecting the data-operation markers and the input/output schemas. We have not yet benchmarked the legibility of large process-plus-data diagrams against the artifacts they replace; the modeler mitigates visual density through collapsible layers (the high-level protocol toggles the data layer off, the full dependency graph toggles it on), and the legibility question itself is one we leave for future readability studies.

[GAP: the worked RT dataset for Figure 8. The model-by-persona-by-task agent-panel pilot (seed 42) is the reproducible anchor; a human battery RT dataset can slot into the same schema when available.]

## 2.8 Model: a machine-learning pipeline in the same notation

The analysis stops at group summaries, but the same trials can feed a model: a classifier of human versus agent, a model of the response-time distribution across tasks and difficulty levels, or, with accompanying neural recordings, a multimodal predictor. ML pipelines face the same fragmentation experimental protocols do: a model card in one repository, feature engineering in another, the training script in a third, deployment config in a fourth, and retraining triggers living, if at all, as cron jobs nobody can find. Studyflow's data operations, gateways, and schema-bound data elements apply to ML pipelines as cleanly as to behavioral analyses; in a Studyflow, an analysis and a training pipeline are the same notation with different operators [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml].

We sketch the most demanding case as **OmniProcess**, a multimodal preprocessing and training pipeline that harmonizes EEG, fMRI, and behavioral recordings across heterogeneous public datasets. The deployed pipeline is forthcoming; the encoding here is the Studyflow diagram that would specify it. OmniProcess specializes the generic process-orchestration and data-transformation layers with concrete neuroimaging primitives: dedicated fMRI and EEG preprocessing activities layered on the generic map, filter, reduce, and transform operators. A canonical OmniProcess Studyflow proceeds in four movements (Figure 11). (1) **Ingest** loads raw recordings from a BIDS-typed data catalog (OpenNeuro, TUH EEG, UK Biobank, ABCD), each registered against a canonical address whose query API lazily materializes derivatives on demand. (2) **Modality-specific preprocessing** runs as parallel subprocesses: fMRI preprocessing chains brain extraction, motion correction, MNI152 registration, and confound removal through fMRIPrep, ANTsPyNet, and Nilearn; EEG preprocessing chains layout normalization, channel selection, filtering, artifact removal, re-referencing, and source localization through MNE and EEGPrep; behavioral data is converted to BDM trials [@defossez2020bdm] with original stimuli, raw responses, and evaluation scores retained, which is exactly the schema the battery's agents wrote to. (3) **Multiverse expansion** captures the multiple defensible analytical paths each preprocessing step admits (a high-pass cutoff at 0.1 Hz versus 0.5 Hz, alternative re-referencing schemes, different brain atlases) as explicit branches off a composed-pipeline marker, so downstream models can compare across choices rather than committing to one [@steegen2016multiverse]. (4) **Harmonized corpus output** writes the preprocessed derivatives back to the catalog under their canonical addresses with schema-bound metadata, which downstream model-training, fine-tuning, and evaluation subprocesses then consume by reading specific addresses without needing to know how they were produced.

Three properties become explicit in this encoding that are hard to recover from prose. **Provenance is the diagram**: every derived artifact traces back to its raw source through the Studyflow nodes that produced it, including the parameterization captured in inline configurations. **Multiverse is first-class**: alternative paths are explicit branches rather than version-controlled forks of a script, so cross-pipeline disagreement reduces to a structured comparison instead of a discovery exercise [@steegen2016multiverse]. **Cross-dataset interoperability is a schema decision**: a preprocessing subprocess defined once targets every dataset whose recordings honor the same format, turning per-dataset engineering into a one-time schema commitment. The same encoding extends to HPC, where subprocesses are containerized (Docker, Apptainer) and scheduled on a SLURM cluster, and to downstream stages: a script activity that consumes the harmonized corpus and emits a model snapshot is a straightforward continuation of the diagram, as are fine-tuning, evaluation, and monitoring subprocesses [@kourani2024promoai]. Planned data-governance operations (anonymize, validate, control access) would make regulatory steps first-class diagram elements rather than annotations [@ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health].

## 2.9 Report and publish: one file against the publication guidelines

The lifecycle closes where it began, at the reporting guidelines that shaped the design. Because the study ran inside the same file, the CONSORT figure is not redrawn at write-up time; the modeler exports it from the protocol that ran the trial, with the attrition counts already written into the boundary error events. The figure that appears in the paper is the file that ran the study, the most direct answer to the "different artifacts drift" failure that motivates this work.

Reporting against a guideline then becomes a property the diagram can be checked for rather than a PDF assembled alongside it. Each guideline is structurally a controlled vocabulary plus a checklist plus, sometimes, a flow diagram, and Studyflow's mechanism is identical across all of them: checklist items become entries in the optional `checklist` attribute on the relevant element, flow diagrams become Studyflow renderings with boundary error events for attrition where applicable, and vocabulary becomes labels on activities, gateways, and data elements. Because the checklist attribute is machine-readable, the Checklist view projects the items as a markdown list with each one linked back to the element that satisfies it, so a study is audited without leaving the diagram. The EQUATOR network catalogs these standards [@simera2010equator]; Table 2 lists the eleven most widely used and Studyflow's current coverage.

| Topic | Guideline | Template ships? | Checklist view? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Randomized trials | CONSORT | Yes | Yes |
| Study protocols | SPIRIT | Yes | Yes |
| Observational studies | STROBE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Systematic reviews | PRISMA | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Diagnostic/prognostic | STARD | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Case reports | CARE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Clinical practice | AGREE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Qualitative research | SRQR | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Animal pre-clinical | ARRIVE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Quality improvement | SQUIRE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Economic evaluations | CHEERS | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |

Two guidelines ship as worked templates today: CONSORT 2025 and SPIRIT 2025. CONSORT 2025's 30-item checklist [@hopewell2025consort] maps onto the shipped CONSORT template, and SPIRIT 2025's 34 items across 9 topics [@chan2025spirit] map onto a Gantt view (Figure 9) that serves at once as the study schedule and the SPIRIT checklist. The other nine are roadmap items rather than gaps in the mechanism: the elements, attributes, and Checklist view are in place, and what remains per guideline is roughly a half-day of authoring, with STROBE and PRISMA next. The pattern recurs across the catalog: PRISMA 2020 [@page2021prisma] standardized the study-flow diagrams that are visual instances of what Studyflow generalizes; TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier] makes participant-facing intervention details first-class items that map almost line by line onto the participant branch; and ARRIVE 2.0 [@percie2020arrive], whose endorsement-without-adherence history is itself one of the strongest arguments for an executable backbone, supplies the animal-research counterpart.

The deeper point is that reporting guidelines and execution specifications need not be different artifacts. A SPIRIT protocol is a *plan* and a CONSORT diagram is a *report*; in current practice the two are written by different people at different times into different files. Encoded as a Studyflow they are the same file at two points in its lifecycle, the schedule before randomization and the flow diagram with attrition counts afterward. At publication the manuscript ships three artifacts that are all views of one source: the exported figure, the Checklist-view audit against the target guideline, and the `.studyflow` file itself paired with the schema-conformant trials table, from which a reader reconstructs what every element and every column means without rerunning the study.

# 3. Discussion

## 3.1 What Studyflow changes

The recurring failure mode in current practice is that the *protocol*, the *pipeline*, and the *figure* are three separate artifacts that begin in agreement and end in drift. Studyflow consolidates these into a single source-of-truth file. The CONSORT diagram is at once the participant-flow figure for the paper, the spec a reviewer can audit against the checklist, and a runnable artifact the runner steps through; the battery is the protocol text, the trial-loop logic, and the executable tasks; the response time pipeline is the analysis section and the transformation script. Drift across these views is no longer possible by construction, because there is only one source. This consolidation yields several advances:

1. **Stakeholder alignment from a single source.** An ethics reviewer, a collaborator, and an engineer read the same diagram at different zoom levels (Study view for procedural structure, Gantt for timing, Checklist for guideline compliance) rather than three documents that disagree subtly.

2. **Versionable, reviewable artifacts.** A Studyflow file is plain BPMN 2.0 XML with stable identifiers, diffs cleanly in Git, and embeds inside an SVG export so the figure in the manuscript carries its own machine-readable source. Procedural specifications come under the same review and version-control discipline that already applies to data and code.

3. **Reusability through specification independence.** Because the language is maintained independently of the modeler (as a LinkML schema), third-party tools (linters, converters, alternative renderers) can target the specification directly without depending on any one application.

4. **Process and data on one diagram.** Data artifacts (datasets, tables, schemas, snapshots) and data operations (map, filter, reduce, group) live alongside the procedure that produced them, so community-schema bindings (BIDS, Psych-DS, BDM, CSVW) attach to specific tasks and the binding survives review.

5. **Reporting-guideline conformance becomes a diagram property.** Checklist items, vocabulary, and flow diagrams from reporting guidelines (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA) map directly to elements of the diagram, so conformance is checkable in the source file rather than against a parallel PDF.

6. **One protocol, many executors.** The same source runs human participants, classic reinforcement-learning agents, and language-model agents through different runtime adapters, so benchmarks for AI systems are no longer authored three times in three different formats; the protocol is the same artifact whose execution is a runtime decision.

The claim underlying all six is **trust by construction**: reproducibility becomes a property of the shared artifact itself rather than add-on documentation. The same diagram that an ethics board approved is the one the participants ran is the one the figures were generated from. That is a stronger guarantee than current practice offers, and the basis on which we expect Studyflow to compose with (rather than compete against) existing reproducibility infrastructure.

## 3.2 Relationship to existing ecosystems

Studyflow sits at the intersection of four ecosystems and does not aim to replace any of them.

**Execution stacks.** Nextflow, the Common Workflow Language (CWL), the Workflow Description Language (WDL), Pegasus, Apache Airflow, Kedro, and domain-specific engines such as NiPype and Pydra solve a problem Studyflow does not: scalable, reproducible execution on heterogeneous compute [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows; @nextflow; @cwl; @pydra]. Their representations are optimized for machines and developers, not for ethics boards or journal reviewers. A more fundamental limitation they share is their reliance on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) as the underlying computational model: DAGs are well-suited to data pipelines with fixed inputs and outputs, but scientific inquiry itself is inherently iterative, since hypothesis generation, experimentation, and revisited analysis form continuous feedback loops that AI-driven discovery systems are beginning to operationalize [@ghareeb2025]. BPMN's sequence flows, boundary events, and choreography express these cycles natively; a DAG-based stack must emulate them through external control logic or repeated workflow executions. Studyflow sits *above* such systems: a Studyflow task can reference an external script (a Nextflow process, a Kedro node, a NiPype workflow) and a downstream tool can compile the protocol-level diagram into an executable graph for one of these engines. The boundary is deliberate: we have prioritized communication over execution [@ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. By the same logic Studyflow does not perform process-mining or post-hoc conformance analysis on runtime traces; those traces conform to a structure that downstream process-mining tools can consume directly [@vanderaalst2016process].

**Data standards.** BIDS, Psych-DS, the Behaverse Data Model, and CSVW prescribe how datasets are structured [@bids; @psychds; @bdm; @csvw]; they say nothing about the process that produced them. Studyflow describes the process and references the data standards through schema-bound dataset, table, and schema elements. The two are complementary: a Studyflow diagram with a BIDS-typed dataset linked to a "Record EEG" task tells the reader (and the machine) both *what* was collected and *how*.

**Reporting guidelines.** CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, STARD, and their siblings [@moher2012; @spirit2013; @strobe; @stard] enforce structure at the publication stage. Today, conformance is checked by hand against PDF supplementary materials. Studyflow can be the carrier for these guidelines: a CONSORT diagram authored as Studyflow carries the checklist items as elements, and the same idea applies to SPIRIT. Conformance becomes a property the diagram can be checked against, not a checklist tacked on afterwards.

**Other BPMN profiles.** BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless ML [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and the human-agent extension [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent] are sibling profiles in adjacent domains. Studyflow's layered schema architecture (core plus a companion cognitive layer and four optional domain layers) follows the same pattern, and we expect future extensions for neuroimaging, clinical neurology, or developmental research to layer in similarly without modifying the core. Visual modeling languages already used in life-sciences-adjacent fields, such as Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009], confirm both the appetite for graphical formalization and the importance of domain-specific vocabulary [@norouzi2025semantic_processes].

Studyflow is also not an ontology of experimental design. Ontologies developed for processes are numerous but suffer from high upfront cost and low reuse [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]; we have aimed instead for a profile that is small enough to learn from one worked example and a glossary, and that is enforced by tooling rather than by inspection.

Across these four ecosystems, a shared architectural pattern makes Studyflow's position concrete. LinkML [@moxon2025linkml], NIDM-Results [@maumet2016nidm], BIDS [@bids], and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis] are not competitors of one another; they occupy *different planes* of the same pattern (a schema layer, a human-friendly authoring layer, and one or more machine-readable outputs) over different aspects of a study: LinkML over the data model, NIDM-Results over analysis outputs, BIDS over multimodal data organization, and ARTEM-IS over methods reporting. The pattern's procedural plane, an end-to-end, machine-readable, human-authorable specification of the study *process*, is the gap Studyflow fills. ARTEM-IS is the closest existing precedent in spirit: it commits the EEG-methods reporting community to structured templates that emit both human-readable forms and JSON, and Studyflow generalizes the same commitment from EEG-methods reporting to whole-study procedural specification. Concrete interoperability follows from this framing rather than competing with it: Studyflow diagrams can emit NIDM-Results-compatible analysis sub-graphs, schema-bind `Dataset` elements to BIDS layouts, express their data plane in LinkML, and export their methods-reporting block as ARTEM-IS-compatible JSON. None of these crosswalks subsumes a neighbor; the value is mutual.

## 3.3 Future directions

The language has near-term extensions queued in the roadmap. Timeseries and event-marker data structures will round out the data taxonomy for physiological and behavioral recordings; explicit storage operations (load, save, export) will separate pure transformations from I/O; data-governance operations (anonymize, validate, access control) will encode regulatory steps as first-class elements rather than annotations; stochastic operators and a tidyverse-mirrored vocabulary (split, clean, join, pivot, select, mutate, summarize) will close the gap with everyday analysis idioms.

Tooling will follow the same path. A dedicated schema editor for data stores is in progress, as are improved inspector ergonomics, additional worked examples (data collection, MLOps, analysis), and a published specification for the data elements. On the runner side, support for parallel gateways, true stratified allocation, and choreography traversal across pools is planned, alongside broader runtime integrations beyond the Behaverse Data Server so that a Studyflow diagram can drive heterogeneous downstream stacks (Kedro, Nextflow, NiPype) [@ghareeb2025].

Some experimental designs are intrinsically awkward to express as directed graphs. Adaptive trials, certain Bayesian sequential designs, and ABAB single-subject designs need representations of feedback, dynamic re-allocation, or open-ended replay loops that exceed what BPMN sequence flow encodes naturally [@ghareeb2025]. The choreography and message-flow elements can express some of this; the rest is current research.

A larger question is community formation. Sibling BPMN profiles in clinical pathways and serverless ML emerged because a small number of groups committed to the same notation; Studyflow's layered design is deliberately set up to make new domain extensions cheap (each is one schema file plus optional renderer code). Adoption beyond our group is still limited; we have tried to lower the bar (MIT-licensed, browser-only deployment, BPMN 2.0 XML on disk, LinkML as the source of truth, no server dependency), but the bar exists nonetheless. External adoption signals are the goal: forks of the modeler for adjacent domains, third-party validators against the LinkML schema, and re-use of the SPIRIT and CONSORT templates in registered reports and journal supplements. [GAP: community-adoption signals (fork counts, external data-server deployments, or third-party Studyflow files in the wild) to be added when available.]

Two lines of empirical work will strengthen the evidence base. First, a readability and comprehension study with 5-10 cognitive scientists comparing Studyflow diagrams against the artifacts they replace (protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, analysis scripts) would test the *trust by construction* claim against measured reviewer effort. Second, end-to-end demonstrations beyond the single study reported here (a multi-session longitudinal study, an ABAB single-subject design, an MLOps pipeline with a fairness audit and retraining loop) would map the boundaries of what the current vocabulary covers. Both are realistic for a follow-up applications paper once Studyflow has been picked up by groups outside our own.

# Code and data availability


All artifacts are open source under the MIT license and run in the browser without installation. The hosted modeler is at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app>, the hosted runner at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/run.html>, and the documentation at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/docs/>. The modeler, runner, the runtime schemas, the example diagrams, and the documentation all live in `github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler`; the canonical LinkML schema is versioned separately at `github.com/behaverse/schemas`.

The versions used in this paper are tagged in the repository; a stable release will be tagged at camera-ready time. End-to-end tests cover the create / inspect / save / load / run round-trip for each example diagram.

Example diagrams referenced in the paper ship with the modeler: a CONSORT 2025-style randomized trial, a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, a base demo, and three agent-profiling demos (`bot_external.studyflow`, a randomized baseline; `bot_claude.studyflow`, a commercial language model; and `bot_ollama.studyflow`, a local open-weight model). Reproducing every figure requires opening the corresponding diagram in the hosted modeler and exporting SVG; runner figures are reproduced by loading the same files into the runner with seed 42. Permanent links to the exact source commits will be added to the camera-ready version.
